KEY MESSAGE 1...

A cold front continues to track eastward across eastern NY this
afternoon with the latest ASOS and NYS mesonet observations 
showing winds shifting to the west in the wake of the front and 
quickly increasing up to 25 to 35mph. The strongest winds have 
been focused in the Mohawk Valley and Capital District thanks to
channeled flow. The front will track into western New England
through the afternoon, ushering in these gusty westerly winds
with the strongest winds likely in western MA. Latest NBM
probabilistic guidance shows a 30 to 50% chance for wind gusts
to exceed 35 mph in parts of Berkshire County, MA but given
limited coverage, will continue to message wind gusts mainly up
to 35 mph. Strongest wind gusts will occur through sunset with
the loss of daytime heating allowing wind gusts to decrease this
evening. 

After daytime temperatures today peak in the 50s to mid 60s, 
westerly winds will advect much cooler temperatures into the 
region tomorrow and Wednesday. The westerly flow and cold air 
advection tonight will support some lake effect rain and wet
snow showers in the Mohawk Valley, western Adirondacks and
northern Catskills. Given marginal temperatures and limited QPF
amounts, overall wet snow accumulations look minor with NBM
probabilistic guidance showing only very low chances (10 - 20%)
of a few tenths of an inch of snow in the southern Adirondacks 
and northern Catskills.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

Large scale Canadian high pressure will dominate the Northeast
on Tuesday and Wednesday resulting in cool and dry conditions for
anyone planning to travel for Thanksgiving. However, there is 
medium to high confidence in yet another coastal storm tracking 
into the Northeast Thanksgiving Day into Thursday night with 
showers lingering in Friday. Unlike our most recent coastal 
storm where the track was highly uncertain, there is rather 
good consensus with this storm tracking further inland as a 
rather potent shortwave trough diving into the Central CONUS 
cuts-off and phases with a southern stream shortwave moving 
across the Gulf Coast States. As the two phase, strong forcing 
for ascent and favorable jet dynamics will allow a secondary 
low to form off the Southeast coast with the parent cyclone 
steering it inland as it approaches the Northeast. East to 
southeasterly winds within the low and mid level jet will 
strengthen as the low deepens, supporting a strong fetch of 
moisture from the Caribbean and western Atlantic that will be 
directed northward. In fact, PWATS and integrated water vapor 
transport within the incoming moisture plume rank within the 
99th percentile of the NAEFS which is notable. There is strong 
consensus among the latest guidance for strong isentropic lift 
along the leading edge of the deepening low to usher in a 
laterally translating band of moderate to locally heavy 
precipitation as it marches from south to north on Thanksgiving.
In terms of timing, large scale high pressure and upper level 
ridging looks to keep eastern NY and western New England dry 
through Thursday morning with precipitation arriving from south 
to north into areas near and south of I-90 Thursday afternoon 
and holding off until late afternoon or even evening for areas 
north. Depending on when folks hit the road for their 
Thanksgiving plans, the incoming precipitation may impact travel
as moderate to locally heavy rain can reduce visibility and 
slow down travel. Leaving in the morning will increases chances 
of dry weather but travelers will encounter precipitation in the
evening as they return home.

The low and mid-level jet ahead of and to the east of the 
incoming storm is quite strong with the 850 hPa and 700 hPa
v-componet of the winds ranking above the 95th percentile of the
NAEFS for this time of year. Such a strong push of warm and
moisture advection in the low and mid-levels will usher a very 
mild air mass northward on Thursday. The delayed arrival time 
should allow the air mass enough time to modify from the cool 
early Thurs A.M temperatures and support mainly plain rain as 
it arrives Thurs P.M/evening. However, the exception continues 
to be higher terrain areas mainly at and above 1000 feet in the 
northern/eastern Catskills, southern Adirondacks, southern 
Greens, Berkshires, and Taconics. Here, low dew point 
temperatures still near or under 32 degrees as moderate to 
locally heavy precip arrives looks to support wet-bulb cooling 
processes that allow a rain/snow mix or even a period of 
moderate wet snow as forecast soundings become isothermal. Any 
periods of moderate wet snow should not be too long-lived as the
impressive low and mid-level jet quickly advects very warm air 
northward, transitioning wet snow or mix over to plain rain by 
Thursday night. Thus, the latest WSSI-P continues to show only a
10 to 30% chance for minor winter weather impacts in these 
higher terrain locations in the 24-hr period ending Fri A.M.
